Hamam al-Hammami, identified as the co-pilot who attacked a flight captain on a flight to Tel Aviv, studied at a UK university prior to the attack, it has emerged.
A spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University told The Independent: "Our thoughts are with the injured pilot, crew and passengers involved in this incident.
"Hamam al Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management. He did not undertake any pilot training at the University."
The UAE's prosecutor general said he intended to carry out a "terror attack" and that the man, who was identified on Saturday as Omani national al-Hammami, used a crash axe to stab the captain.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.
Hammami was born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother, CNN quoted sources and Israeli officials familiar with the matter as saying.
He was banned from flying last year over concerns that he had radical ideological views, according to Saudi state media.
FlyDubai has said that the incident is still under investigation.
Breaking: Israeli hijacking co-pilot completed course at UK university
Hamam al-Hammami, a co-pilot who attacked a flight captain on a flight to Tel Aviv, completed a course at Buckinghamshire New University it has emerged.
A spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University told The Independent: "Our thoughts are with the injured pilot, crew and passengers involved in this incident.
"Hamam al Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management. He did not undertake any pilot training at the University."
Polanski says Israel has 'definitely' operated false flag operations
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said that Israel has "definitely" conducted false flag operations in the past.
"What I find really difficult to navigate is anti-Semitism on the Left," he said in an episode of the Bold Politics podcast.
"Because, again, I want to be really clear: there are definitely examples of where the Israeli government [has] used false flags."
It comes amid a row about anti-semitism in the party.
How a six-year-old girl helped avert Israel flight disaster after pilot stabbed
A six-year-old girl played a crucial role in preventing a major disaster when a co-pilot attacked a flight captain on board a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday.
Nina Manes happened to ask her mother Tali to take her to the lavatory on board the flight just as the man, who is an Omani national but has not been named, attacked Indian Cpt Smit Machchhar by stabbing him repeatedly.
Air travel expert gives verdict on three key issues of the Flydubai plane hijacking
The alleged hijacking of an Israel-bound flight has raised questions over how secure the vetting process is for one of aviation's most skilled jobs.
Flydubai FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv rapidly descended during a terrifying ordeal as the co-pilot allegedly tried to take control of the plane after attacking his fellow pilot with an axe, or possibly stabbing him.
It is still unclear why the co-pilot to acted in this way. Yet the question remains: how was this person able to bypass rigorous background checks and be given the responsibility of flying planes?
"It's very easy after every incident to say, what more can we do?" Phillip Baum, visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said.
"Often, airline pilots are recruited from other states, so the degree of background checks is somewhat limited. They'll certainly have their pilot training and licenses, but in terms of background checks from other states, it's always a problem."
Israeli officials expected to question co-pilot of FlyDubai flight
Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial passenger flight from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation.
Disaster was averted on FlyDubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had stabbed the captain in what Israeli officials have said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying over 170 passengers and crew.
The co-pilot was transferred on Thursday to the UAE, where the source said Israeli officials were expected to question him.
The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part in the questioning.
Asked whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot, an Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.
Israel plane attacker was banned from flying by Oman over suspected radicalisation - report
The FlyDubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain had previously been banned from flying over concerns he had radical ideological views, it has been reported.
Though the pilot- an Omani national - was banned by his country, he was still hired by FlyDubai, according to the Wall Street Journal.
However, the nature of his radicalisation has not been shared.
Iran denies involvement in RAF Fairford air base security incidents
The leaders of Britain and the United States have suggested, without giving evidence, that Iran played a role in two major security incidents this week, the arrests near a US-run military base in England used in the war against Tehran and the attack in the cockpit of an Israel-bound plane.
As of Friday, no confirmed connection to the Islamic Republic had emerged.
Britain has not made public any evidence linking Iran to the air-base arrests on terrorism-related charges.
And an official who was not authorized to speak to the media said there is currently no evidence of a link between Iran and the cockpit attack.
The investigations are in the early stages.
If an Iranian link to the Britain arrests is confirmed, it would underline a strategy that Iran's government has promoted for decades, using smaller, relatively low-cost attacks to needle and disrupt more powerful adversaries and their economies while causing friction among allies.
Iran has denied involvement in Sunday's arrests close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.
Iranian leaders summoned Britain's ambassador and called on the British government to provide an official explanation.
Police on Thursday arrested a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian citizen on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, while five other suspects were released on bail.
Detectives said they found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in vans near the air base, but no explosives.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident but did not provide details.
Flydubai co-pilot attacked pilot with axe in attempted 'terrorist' attack, UAE says
An Omani co-pilot on FlyDubai flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a "terrorist" attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.
The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with an axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.
Boston native recalls moment plane started to plummet
Boston native Mika Bauman tells NBC News an 11-year-old girl who was sitting next to her grabbed her hand as the FlyDubai plane started to plummet.
"We just held hands, me and her, and her father next to her, and we all screamed," she said.
"We didn't let go until Saudi Arabia."
Bauman is a dual US-Israeli citizen who was flying home to Tel Aviv.

A FlyDubai co-pilot who attempted to hijack a Tel Aviv-bound passenger jet with a cockpit crash axe studied at a British university.
Hamam al-Hammami, 29, earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023. The UK institution has since said that the qualification involved no practical flight training.
Earlier reporting byThe Independent confirmed that Mr al-Hammami is an Omani national born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother.
A spokesperson for the university told Press Association: "Our thoughts are with the injured pilot, crew and passengers involved in this incident.
"Hamam al Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management. He did not undertake any pilot training at the University."
Mr al-Hammami was reportedly banned from flying by Omani authorities last year due to his radical views. Following his detention he allegedly told investigators that he intended to crash the airliner in Israel.
The revelations come as Israeli investigators arrived in the UAE on Saturday to interrogate the suspect.
Authorities from both nations are focusing on whether Mr al-Hammami operated independently as a "lone wolf" or under the direction of an external extremist network.
According to accounts obtained by Emirati prosecutors, two hours into Wednesday's flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Hammami seized the emergency axe and repeatedly slashed Indian captain Smit Machchhar.
The struggle sent the Boeing 737 MAX into a sudden 17,000-foot plunge toward the Gulf.
Despite sustaining severe injuries, Captain Machchhar has said he was able to unlock the flight deck door, allowing passengers to force their way inside, subdue Hammami, and stabilise the aircraft before making an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Speaking to reporters, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed intelligence services are investigating whether Mr al-Hammami operated under external direction, warning that any accomplices would pay a "heavy price."
As speculation surrounding Mr al-Hammami motives heightens, former US diplomats and regional analysts have suggested the attack carried a "dual target," and may have been a deliberate attempt to derail the 2020 Abraham Accords, which established commercial air routes between Israel and Gulf states.
The joint investigation is currently focused on how Mr al-Hammami passed employment background checks.
Oman Air previously removed Hammami from flight duties after intelligence officials discovered extremist materials on his devices and noted visits to radical websites, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal and ABC News.
It remains unclear whether Omani officials shared these security concerns with neighbouring states or international carriers.
Mr al-Hammami was later transferred to an administrative desk job before briefly training at Royal Air Maroc, which ultimately rejected his application. FlyDubai then hired him eight months ago.
Former Israeli intelligence officials have said that allowing a national from a country with no diplomatic ties to Israel onto the Tel Aviv route represents a critical failure by Israeli and Emirati security agencies.
Following the incident, regional aviation authorities have launched urgent reviews of all aircrew screening protocols.
